blocks.main: **In a mass-spring system, a mass is attached to a spring, and together they vibrate around a resting position.** This resting position is called **equilibrium** (the position where the spring is neither stretched nor compressed). The spring always pulls the mass back toward equilibrium. The moving mass tends to **keep moving**, so it goes past equilibrium. Then the spring pulls it back again, and the cycle repeats.
sub: The vibration can be **longitudinal** (back and forth along the length of the spring) or **transverse** (up and down, across the spring).
Both directions work the same way, because in each one the same spring pulls the same mass back.
blocks.end: So the mass keeps vibrating because the spring keeps pulling it back and the mass keeps going past equilibrium.

blocks.main: **In a mass-spring system, the frequency depends on the mass and on the stiffness of the spring.** **Frequency** is how many times the system goes back and forth each second. **Stiffness** is how hard the spring pulls back when it is stretched or compressed. **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
sub: A heavier mass is harder to get moving and harder to turn around. So each cycle takes longer, and the frequency goes down.
A stiffer spring pulls back harder, so the mass returns faster. Each cycle takes less time, so the frequency goes up.
blocks.end: So mass and stiffness change the frequency in opposite directions.

blocks.main: **When two masses are joined by springs, the system can vibrate in two different ways, called modes.** A **mode** is one way a system can vibrate. In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together, in the same direction at the same time. In **Mode 2**, the two masses move against each other, in opposite directions.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the middle spring hardly stretches, because both masses move together. So it adds little stiffness, and **the frequency is lower**.
In **Mode 2**, the middle spring stretches and compresses a lot, because the masses move in opposite directions. So it adds stiffness, and **the frequency is higher**.
The more the masses move **against each other**, the more the springs stretch and compress. So more stiffness is working in that mode, and it has a **higher frequency**.
blocks.end: So a higher mode vibrates faster because more of the springs stretch and compress.

blocks.main: **Three masses joined by springs have three modes.** In **Mode 1**, all three masses move together. In **Mode 2**, the middle mass stays still, and the two outer masses move against each other. In **Mode 3**, the middle mass moves in the opposite direction from both outer masses.
sub: **A mass changes the frequency only if it moves in that mode, and a spring changes the frequency only if it stretches in that mode.**

If the middle mass is made heavier, **Mode 1 and Mode 3 have lower frequencies**. This is because the middle mass moves in both of those modes. A heavier mass is harder to move, so those modes vibrate more slowly.
The same heavier middle mass **does not change Mode 2**, because the middle mass does not move in Mode 2.
blocks.end: So Mode 3 stretches the springs the most, because each mass moves against its neighbor. That is why Mode 3 has the highest frequency.

blocks.ref: Lecture 11 · p7 · Lecture 12 · p7 · Lecture 13 · p3
blocks.main: **Each mass added to the chain creates one more mode, so N masses have N modes.** The same patterns repeat as the chain gets longer. Lower modes have broad movements, where large sections of the chain move in the same direction. In higher modes, the direction of movement changes more often along the chain.
sub: An infinite number of masses and springs along a line is a **string**.
An infinite number of masses and springs spread over a surface is a **membrane**, such as a drum or the vocal folds.
A string or a membrane can vibrate in several modes at the same time.
blocks.end: So a string and the vocal folds each have a whole series of modes.

questions.q: Why do multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies?
questions.a: Multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies because they can vibrate in several different modes (ways of vibrating), and each mode has its own frequency. This is because the masses can move in different ways. In some modes the masses move together, and in others they move against each other. When the masses move against each other, the springs between them stretch and compress more. So more stiffness is working, and that mode vibrates faster. So a system with N masses has N modes and N frequencies.

questions.q: How many modes does a 3-mass system have?
questions.a: A 3-mass system has three modes. This is because a system with N masses has N modes of vibration. So 3 masses give 3 modes.

questions.q: Four masses are joined by springs between two walls. How many modes does the system have, and what are the masses doing in the lowest and highest modes?
questions.a:
The system has four modes. This is because there is one mode for each mass, and there are four masses.

In the lowest mode, Mode 1, all four masses move in the same direction at the same time.

In the highest mode, Mode 4, every mass moves in the opposite direction from its neighbors. Because of this, every spring is stretched and compressed. So the most stiffness is working, and the frequency is highest.

questions.q: Which mode of the 3-mass system has the highest frequency? Why?
questions.a: Mode 3 has the highest frequency of the 3-mass system. This is because in Mode 3 the middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses. So every spring is stretched and compressed as much as possible. That means the most stiffness is working, and more stiffness makes the system vibrate faster. So Mode 3 vibrates fastest and has the highest frequency.

questions.q: Which mode of a 2-mass system has the lowest frequency, and why?
questions.a: Mode 1 has the lowest frequency of a 2-mass system. This is because in Mode 1 the two masses move together. So the middle spring moves along with them without stretching. Only the two outer springs are stretching and compressing. So Mode 1 has less stiffness working than Mode 2, and it vibrates more slowly.

questions.q: If you increase mass 2, what happens to the frequencies of each of the modes?
questions.a: If you increase mass 2, the frequencies of Mode 1 and Mode 3 go down, and the frequency of Mode 2 stays the same. This is because mass 2 is the middle mass, and it moves in Mode 1 and in Mode 3. A heavier mass is harder to move, so those two modes vibrate more slowly, and their frequencies go down. In Mode 2, the middle mass does not move. A mass that does not move has no effect on the frequency, so Mode 2 stays the same.

questions.q: In the 3-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make mass 1 (an outer mass) heavier?
questions.a: All three modes have lower frequencies when mass 1 becomes heavier. This is because mass 1 moves in all three modes. When a mass becomes heavier, it is harder to move, so the system vibrates more slowly. Since mass 1 moves in every mode, all three modes slow down, and their frequencies decrease.

questions.q: In a 2-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make the middle spring stiffer?
questions.a: When the middle spring of a 2-mass system is made stiffer, Mode 1 stays the same and Mode 2 goes up. This is because in Mode 1 the masses move together, so the middle spring is never stretched. A spring that is not stretched does not affect the frequency, so its extra stiffness does nothing. In Mode 2 the masses move against each other, so the middle spring is stretched and compressed. A stiffer spring pulls back harder, so Mode 2 vibrates faster, and its frequency goes up.

questions.q: What do you get when you have an infinite number of masses and springs?
questions.a: An infinite number of masses and springs gives you a string, such as a guitar or piano string. This is because every small piece of a string has mass, and every small piece stretches the way a spring does. So a string vibrates in modes the same way a chain of masses does, only with infinitely many masses and springs. When the masses and springs are spread over a surface instead of along a line, the result is a membrane, such as a drum or the vocal folds.

questions.q: What happens to the frequency of a single mass on a spring if you make the spring stiffer? If you make the mass heavier?
questions.a:
If you make the spring stiffer, the frequency of a single mass on a spring goes up. This is because a stiffer spring pulls the mass back toward equilibrium (its resting position) with more force. So the mass turns around sooner, and each cycle takes less time.

If you make the mass heavier, the frequency goes down. This is because a heavier mass is harder to start and stop. So each back-and-forth cycle takes longer, and the system vibrates more slowly.

topics.title: Neural networks: inner products, weights and decisions

blocks.main: **The vowel network is a neural network that takes in a vowel as two numbers and picks a word.** The two input numbers are **F1 and F2** (the first and second formants, which are frequency regions with strong acoustic energy). The network chooses among five words, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
sub: A low F1 and a high F2 is the vowel /i/, so the correct answer for that input is dean.
blocks.end: So the whole network turns two formant values into one choice among five words.

blocks.main: **Each neuron in the network multiplies each incoming activation by its weight and adds up the results.** An incoming **activation** is a number that comes into the neuron from the layer before it. This sum is called the **inner product**, and it is the core calculation of all AI. A **weight** is a positive or negative number that determines how much an input counts.
sub: A positive weight leaves the sign of the input the same, so a positive input stays positive. A negative weight changes the sign to the opposite. For example, if the input is +3, a weight of +2 gives +6, so it stays positive. A weight of −2 gives −6, so it becomes negative.
**The network's knowledge is stored in its weights**, so learning means changing the weights.
blocks.end: So the weights start out random and become useful through learning.

blocks.ref: Lecture 14 · p24 · Lecture 15 · p3 · Lecture 16 · p3
blocks.main: **Forward propagation passes the inner products layer by layer, from the input to the output.** The input layer provides F1 and F2. Each later layer takes the activations from the layer before it, calculates its own results, and passes them on to the next layer.
sub: The output layer gives one number for each of the five words.
blocks.end: So a **forward pass** uses the network's current weights to make a guess. The network can make this guess even before it has learned good weights, but then the guess may be wrong.

blocks.main: **The output of the vowel network is a probability distribution over the five words.** A **probability distribution** is a list of probabilities, one for each word. Each number is between 0 and 1, and the numbers **add up to 1**. The word with the largest number is the network's decision.
sub: The correct answer is written as a **one-hot** list, which has a 1 for the correct word and a 0 for every other word.
For dean, the one-hot list is 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, because dean is the third of the five words.
blocks.end: So the outputs can add up to 1 and still put the most probability on the wrong word.

blocks.main: **Whether an output increases or decreases depends on whether the activation and weight are positive or negative.** When both are positive, increasing either one makes the output's probability go **up**. This is because a positive activation times a positive weight gives a positive number, so making either one larger makes that number larger.
sub: If the weight is negative, increasing the positive activation makes that output's probability go **down**.

questions.q: If an activation of 1.57 feeds the done output through a weight of positive 0.1, what happens to the probability of done if the weight goes up? If the activation goes up?
questions.a:
If the weight goes up, the probability of done goes up. This is because the contribution to the done output is the activation times the weight. The activation, 1.57, and the weight, 0.1, are both positive. So a larger weight makes the product larger, and the probability of done goes up.

If the activation goes up, the probability of done also goes up. This is because the weight is still positive, so a larger positive activation also makes the product larger.

Only the signs matter here, so you do not need to do the multiplication.

questions.q: What happens to the probability of done if that same weight were negative and the activation went up?
questions.a: If that same weight were negative and the activation went up, the probability of done would go down. This is because a positive activation times a negative weight gives a negative number. A larger activation makes that number more negative. For example, 1.57 times −0.1 gives −0.157, and 2 times −0.1 gives −0.2. So the contribution to the done output becomes more negative, and the probability of done goes down.

questions.q: Is 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 a valid probability distribution?
questions.a: No, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 is not a valid probability distribution. This is because these numbers add up to 1.1. A probability distribution must add up to exactly 1. So this list is not valid, because its total is 0.1 too high.

questions.q: The first of five categories is correct. Write the desired output.
questions.a: The desired output (the correct answer the network should give) is 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. This is because the first category is correct, so it gets a 1. Every other category is wrong, so each one gets a 0. So all of the probability is on the correct category.

questions.q: The desired output over done, dune, dean, Don, Dan is 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, and the network outputs 0.10, 0.15, 0.60, 0.10, 0.05. Which vowel was said, which did the network guess, and what is the loss?
questions.a:
Don was said. This is because the desired output, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, has its 1 in the fourth position, and Don is the fourth word.

The network guessed dean. This is because dean has the largest probability in the network's output, 0.60.

The loss is a number that measures how far the computed output is from the desired output. For example, it measures how much probability the network put on dean, where the desired output has a 0.

questions.q: What does Linear mean in the network code?
questions.a: In the network code, Linear means the layer computes inner products. Each neuron multiplies each incoming number by its weight and adds up the results. A Linear layer does nothing else after that. So its outputs are just those sums.

topics.title: Training results: chance, overlap and repeated runs

blocks.main: **The vowel network is trained on a table of real vowel recordings, and each row of formants is paired with its vowel.** The input table has two columns, F1 and F2 (the first and second formants). The target table (the table of correct answers) has five columns, one for each word.
sub: For dean, the target row has a 1 in the dean column and a 0 in every other column.
If the rows got mixed up, each row of formants would be paired with the wrong vowel. So the network would learn the wrong word for those formants.

blocks.main: **When the F1 and F2 values of real speakers are plotted, the vowels overlap a lot.** Each dot on the plot is one recording. Recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 can be different vowels.
sub: **Peterson and Barney** found this overlap in the early 1950s.
Even a person would have to guess for a point in the middle of the overlap.
blocks.end: So one pair of formant values does not always belong to just one vowel.

blocks.main: **Accuracy is how often the network picks the right word, and it starts at chance.** Chance is the accuracy you get by guessing at random. With random weights, the network knows nothing, so it can only guess. A random guess among **five** vowels is right one time in five, so accuracy starts at **20 percent**.
sub: With ten categories, chance would be 10 percent, because a random guess would be right one time in ten.
Each pass of learning is called an **epoch**, and a problem like this takes thousands of epochs.
The network jumps to about 40 percent and levels off near **45 percent**. It stops there because the real vowel data **overlap** so much.

blocks.main: **Ten training runs that start from different random weights take different paths but end at the same accuracy.** Each run begins with its own random weights, so each one learns along its own path.
sub: Children are similar, because they hear different input but learn the same language.

blocks.main: **Children learning English first use forms from memory and later learn the pattern behind them, as Carol Chomsky observed.** At first, children say went correctly because they have memorized it. Then they learn the pattern of adding -ed for the past tense, so they start saying goed.
sub: Later they learn that went is an exception to the pattern.

questions.q: Why does accuracy start at 20 percent?
questions.a: Accuracy starts at 20 percent because the network's first guesses are no better than chance. This is because the network starts with random weights, so it knows nothing. Guessing at random among five vowels is right one time in five. One in five is 20 percent, so that is where accuracy starts.

questions.q: Why does accuracy start at 10 percent for a network with ten output categories?
questions.a: Accuracy starts at 10 percent for a network with ten output categories because its first guesses are no better than chance. This is because a network with random weights knows nothing yet. A random guess among ten categories is right one time in ten. One in ten is 10 percent, so that is where accuracy starts.

questions.q: Why does the vowel network level off near 40 to 45 percent instead of 100 percent?
questions.a: The vowel network levels off near 40 to 45 percent instead of 100 percent because the real formant data for the five vowels overlap a great deal. This is because many recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 belong to different vowels. For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person would have to guess. So no network can classify those points reliably, and accuracy stays well below 100 percent.

questions.q: Ten training runs start from different random weights. What happens?
questions.a: When ten training runs start from different random weights, all ten end at about the same accuracy, even though they take different paths. This is because stochastic gradient descent (SGD, the method that updates the weights in small steps) involves chance along the way. So some runs jump up early, and some stay at chance longer. The end point is still the same for all ten runs.

topics.title: Gestalt completion and the cloze test

blocks.main: **Gestalt psychology studies how people see whole patterns.** In the Gestalt figure, people see a triangle even though no triangle is drawn. They see it because a large part of human knowledge is completing what is missing.
sub: **Closure** is the Gestalt term for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished. For example, people see a broken circle as a whole circle.

blocks.main: **In a cloze test, words are removed from a text, and people fill them in.** The name cloze comes from closure. The test measures knowledge by asking someone to complete a sequence.
sub: An LLM (large language model) that predicts the next word is doing a cloze test again and again.
blocks.end: So training a system only to predict the missing piece turns out to copy human thinking.

questions.q: Describe the Gestalt principle of closure, and how an LLM uses it to learn.
questions.a:
The Gestalt principle of closure is completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished. For example, people see a triangle where none is drawn, and they see a broken circle as a whole circle.

An LLM (large language model) uses closure to learn by doing the same kind of completion. It predicts the missing next piece of a sequence again and again. When its prediction is wrong, it corrects its weights. So it learns by completing sequences over and over.

questions.q: What is a cloze test, and why is an LLM's training like one?
questions.a:
A cloze test is a test where words are removed from a text and people fill them in. So it tests knowledge by asking someone to complete a sequence.

An LLM's training is like a cloze test because the LLM (large language model) is trained by filling in the next word over and over. So for an LLM, knowing something means being able to complete the sequence.

questions.q: Why do people see a triangle in the Gestalt figure?
questions.a: People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure because they complete the missing parts of a familiar pattern. No triangle is actually drawn, but people fill in what is missing. This completion is the Gestalt principle of closure.

blocks.main: **An agentic system is a group of LLMs (large language models) connected so that one LLM's output becomes the next LLM's input.** In AI today, an **agent** is just an LLM. In one example, an outline LLM plans the answer, and a writing LLM writes it.
sub: A critic LLM checks the draft, and a revision LLM works back and forth with the critic.
A final LLM produces the answer that the user sees.

blocks.main: **The critic loop sends the draft back and forth between the critic and the reviser.** The loop continues until the critic is satisfied or a limit is reached. This loop greatly reduced **hallucination** (when an LLM makes up false statements).
sub: Once each LLM is trained, its weights usually do not change.
The agents share a common memory, where they write and read information.

blocks.main: **Software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 are three ways to build a program.** **Software 1.0** is writing a program in a programming language such as Python. **Software 2.0** is training a neural network on input and output data, so the program is the network's weights.
sub: **Software 3.0** is having an agentic system build and run the program from instructions written in plain English.
Building a program this way is called **vibe coding**.

questions.q: What is an agentic system, in terms of LLMs? Describe the example system.
questions.a:
An agentic system is a graph (a set of connected parts) of LLMs (large language models), each with its own job. The LLMs are connected so that one LLM's output becomes the next LLM's input.

In the example system, one LLM outlines, one writes, one critiques, one revises and one produces the final version. The critic and the reviser form a loop. So the draft keeps going back until the critic is satisfied or the limit is reached.

questions.q: What does the critic loop do, and what does it prevent that was common in earlier LLMs?
questions.a:
The critic loop sends the draft back and forth between the critic and the reviser until the critic is satisfied. The critic checks each draft, and the reviser fixes the errors the critic finds. So errors are caught and fixed before the answer is shown to the user.

The critic loop prevents hallucination (when an LLM makes up false statements), which was a common problem in earlier LLMs.

questions.q: What would happen if the critic LLM were removed?
questions.a: If the critic LLM were removed, the draft would go straight from writing to the final answer without being checked. This is because the critic is the LLM that checks the draft. So more made-up statements would reach the user. The critic loop is what greatly reduced hallucination, so without it that reduction would be lost.

questions.q: What is the difference between Software 2.0 and Software 3.0?
questions.a:
The difference between Software 2.0 and Software 3.0 is how the program gets built.

In Software 2.0, a neural network is trained on input and output data, so the program is the network's weights.

In Software 3.0, an agentic system builds and runs the program from plain English instructions. Building a program this way is called vibe coding.

topics.title: Where the springiness is, and what a local change does

blocks.main: **In a vibrating system such as a string or a chain of masses, each spot in a mode is either mostly moving or mostly stretching.** A **mode** is one of the patterns in which the system can vibrate. **Where the system moves the most, it stretches the least.** Where it does not move, it stretches the most. So the springiest spots are the points of **no movement**.
sub: The points of no movement are the fixed ends and the points where the mode crosses its resting line. The resting line is the straight line where the system sits when it is not vibrating.
A **fixed end is always springy** in every mode. This is because the system is held in place there, so it cannot move.
A **free end is always moving** in every mode. This is because nothing holds it in place.
blocks.end: So along the system, moving spots and springy spots alternate, one after the other.

blocks.main: **A small change at one spot affects each mode depending on what that spot is doing in that mode.** Extra mass lowers a mode's frequency (how fast it vibrates) **only where that mode is moving**. Extra stiffness (how strongly the material resists being stretched) raises a mode's frequency **only where that mode is stretching**.
sub: At a spot with lots of motion and little stretching, the extra mass matters. The heavier spot is harder to move, so the system vibrates more slowly, and **the frequency goes down**.
At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, the extra stiffness matters. A stiffer spot pulls back harder when it is stretched, so the system vibrates faster, and **the frequency goes up**.
Adding mass and stiffness at the same spot does **not** cancel out. This is because at one spot in one mode, only one of the two matters. The only exception is a single mass on a single spring.
blocks.end: So the same change can raise the frequency of one mode and lower the frequency of another.

blocks.main: **Perturbation theory predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates.** In the late nineteenth century, researchers tested this by placing small amounts of wax on different parts of a drum.
sub: When wax was placed where the drum vibrated a lot, the extra mass made that part harder to move. So the drum vibrated more slowly, and its frequency (pitch) went down.
When wax was placed where the drum did not vibrate, it had no effect on the drum's frequency or sound.
blocks.end: So the wax changed the frequency only where the drum was moving.

questions.q: This is Mode 5 of a string fixed at both ends. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
questions.a: The areas with the most springiness in Mode 5 are the two fixed ends and the four points where the string crosses its middle line. So six places should be circled. This is because the string does not move at those points. The pieces of string on either side of each point move in opposite directions. So the string at that point is stretched and compressed the most. The tops of the five bumps have the most motion and the least springiness, so they are not circled.

questions.q: This is Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends. Where is the most springiness, and where is the most motion?
questions.a:
The most springiness in Mode 3 is at the two fixed ends and at the two points where the string crosses its middle line. That makes four places in all. This is because the string does not move at those points. So the string is stretched and compressed the most there.

The most motion in Mode 3 is at the tops of the three bumps. This is because the string swings the most there and is hardly stretched.

questions.q: This picture shows Mode 4 of a building. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
questions.a: The areas with the most springiness in Mode 4 of the building are the fixed base and the three points where the building crosses its resting position. So four places should be circled. This is because those points do not move. The parts of the building above and below each point move in opposite directions. So the structure there stretches and compresses the most. The free top moves the most and is the least springy, so it is not circled.

questions.q: This diagram shows Mode 2 of a building. Where is the most springiness?
questions.a: The most springiness in Mode 2 of the building is at the fixed base and at the one point above it where the building crosses its resting position. This is because those two points do not move. So the structure there is stretched and compressed the most. The free top moves the most, so it is the least springy.

questions.q: If we increase the stiffness and mass of the string at the boxed location (where Mode 3 crosses its middle line and Mode 4 is at the top of a bump), what happens to Mode 3 and Mode 4's frequencies, and why?
questions.a:
Mode 3's frequency goes up and Mode 4's frequency goes down when stiffness and mass are increased at the boxed location.

Mode 3's frequency goes up. This is because the boxed spot does not move in Mode 3, but it is stretched the most. The added mass does nothing, because the spot does not move. The added stiffness makes the string pull back harder at that spot, so it vibrates faster.

Mode 4's frequency goes down. This is because the boxed spot moves the most in Mode 4 and is not stretched. The added mass makes the spot harder to move, so the string vibrates more slowly. The added stiffness does nothing, because the spot is not stretched.

questions.q: The box is moved to a spot where Mode 3 moves the most and Mode 4 crosses its middle line. Mass and stiffness are added there. What happens?
questions.a:
When the box is moved to that spot and mass and stiffness are added there, Mode 3's frequency goes down and Mode 4's frequency goes up.

Mode 3's frequency goes down. This is because the spot moves the most in Mode 3 and is hardly stretched. The added mass makes the spot harder to move, so the string vibrates more slowly.

Mode 4's frequency goes up. This is because the spot does not move in Mode 4, but it is stretched the most. The added stiffness makes the string pull back harder at that spot, so it vibrates faster.

questions.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very top, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
questions.a: Increasing the mass and stiffness at the very top of the building makes the frequency of Mode 4 go down. This is because the top of the building is the free end. A free end moves the most in every mode and is hardly stretched. So the added mass counts there. The heavier top is harder to move, so the building vibrates more slowly, and the frequency goes down. The added stiffness does nothing, because nothing is stretching at the top.

questions.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very base, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
questions.a: Increasing the mass and stiffness at the very base of the building makes the frequency of Mode 4 go up. This is because the base is the fixed end. The base never moves, but it is always stretched and compressed. The added mass does nothing there, because the base does not move. The added stiffness makes the structure pull back harder when it is stretched, so it vibrates faster, and the frequency goes up.

questions.q: In Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends, point B does not move and point C is at the bottom of a bump. What happens to Mode 3 if you add a small weight at B? At C? If you stiffen the string at B?
questions.a:
A weight at B leaves Mode 3's frequency the same. This is because B does not move in Mode 3, so the extra mass does not affect the vibration.

A weight at C lowers Mode 3's frequency. This is because C swings the most in Mode 3. The extra mass makes that spot harder to move, so the string vibrates more slowly.

Stiffening the string at B raises Mode 3's frequency. This is because B is where the string stretches the most in Mode 3. A stiffer string pulls back harder when it is stretched, so it vibrates faster.

questions.q: The same spot B is moving in Mode 1. Does a weight at B change Mode 1's frequency?
questions.a: Yes, a weight at B changes Mode 1's frequency, and it makes it go down. This is because in Mode 1 the whole string is one bump, so the spot at B is moving. Extra mass at a moving spot makes it harder to move, so the string vibrates more slowly. So even though B does not move in Mode 3, a weight there lowers the frequency of Mode 1.

blocks.main: **Speech is made by a source and a filter, and the source is the vocal folds.** **F0** is the base frequency, the rate at which the vocal folds vibrate. The vocal folds produce **harmonics**, which are frequencies at whole-number multiples of F0 (1 times F0, 2 times F0, 3 times F0, and so on). With an F0 of 150 Hz, the first five harmonics are 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz.
sub: Heavy, loose vocal folds vibrate slowly, so they give a **low F0**.
Tight, light vocal folds vibrate quickly, so they give a **high F0**. Because the harmonics are multiples of F0, they are then spaced farther apart.
blocks.end: So F0 determines how far apart the harmonics are.

blocks.main: **The filter is the air in the vocal tract, and its formants determine which harmonics come out loud.** **Formants** are frequency regions where the vocal tract makes the sound strongest. **A formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder, and harmonics far from any formant come out weaker.** The **envelope** is the outline traced over the heights of the harmonics, and its peaks show where the formants are.
sub: When F0 stays the same, the harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel, and only their heights change.
The envelope is what makes each vowel sound different from the others.
Changing F0 changes the spacing of the harmonics, but the vowel stays the same.
blocks.end: So pitch and vowel are separate, because the source determines the harmonics and the filter determines the envelope.

blocks.main: **A high F0 spreads the harmonics far apart, so few harmonics fall near each formant.** A low voice has many harmonics close together near each formant, so the envelope shows clearly. A high voice has only a few harmonics near each formant, so the formants are hard to see.
sub: The vocal tract still has its formants. There are just not enough harmonics near them to show the envelope.
blocks.end: So a toddler's or a soprano's vowels are hard to identify.

blocks.main: **F0 also helps express meaning in speech.** F0 falls at the end of a statement and rises at the end of a question.
sub: F0 also signals sarcasm or pretending.

questions.q: What does the source supply and what does the filter do in speech?
questions.a:
The source in speech is the vocal folds, and it supplies the harmonics. The harmonics are frequencies at whole-number multiples of F0 (1 times F0, 2 times F0, and so on).

The filter in speech is the air in the vocal tract, and it determines which harmonics come out loud. This is because its formants make the harmonics near them louder and the harmonics far from them weaker.

So the source determines which frequencies are present, and the filter determines which of them are loud.

questions.q: Two vowels are said at the same pitch. What is the same and what is different in their spectra?
questions.a:
When two vowels are said at the same pitch, the harmonics in their spectra are the same, but the heights of the harmonics are different. A spectrum is a graph of how strong each frequency in the sound is.

The harmonics are the same because the vocal folds vibrate at the same F0 for both vowels. The harmonics are multiples of F0, so the same F0 gives the same harmonics.

The heights are different because each vowel has its constriction (narrowing) in a different place in the vocal tract. So the formants move to different frequencies, and the envelope changes.

questions.q: Why are a toddler's vowels hard to identify?
questions.a: A toddler's vowels are hard to identify because a toddler has a very high F0, so the harmonics are spaced far apart. This means few harmonics fall near each formant. A formant can even fall between two harmonics. So the envelope is hard to see. The formants are still there, but there are too few harmonics to reveal them.

questions.q: If the vocal folds become tighter, what happens to F0 and to the spacing of the harmonics?
questions.a:
When the vocal folds become tighter, F0 goes up and the harmonics are spaced farther apart.

F0 goes up because tighter vocal folds are stiffer. More stiffness raises the frequency, so the vocal folds vibrate faster.

The spacing of the harmonics gets wider because the harmonics are multiples of F0. For example, with an F0 of 100 Hz the harmonics are 100, 200 and 300 Hz. With an F0 of 200 Hz they are 200, 400 and 600 Hz. So when F0 goes up, the harmonics spread farther apart.

blocks.ref: Lecture 14 · p22 · Lecture 15 · p2 · Lecture 16 · p2
blocks.main: **The vowel network is written in PyTorch (a Python library for building neural networks) as a short list of layers.** The network has 2 inputs, three hidden layers (layers between the input and the output) of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 outputs. The 2 inputs are F1 and F2 (the first two formant frequencies of the vowel), and the 5 outputs are the five words.
sub: The import lines bring in the **torch library**, which already contains the programs for inner products and backpropagation. An inner product multiplies each input by its weight and adds up the results. Backpropagation figures out how much each weight contributed to the error.
So none of that math has to be written by hand.

blocks.main: **In the code, nn.Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another.** Each nn.Linear line is a processing layer that computes inner products. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** is a layer that takes input from 2 neurons and has 3 neurons.
sub: The first number on each line must be the same as the second number on the line before it. This is because each layer takes in as many numbers as the layer before it produces. The vowel network has Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4) and Linear(4, 5).
The **input layer gets no line**, because it does no processing. The **last line is always the output layer**.
nn.Sigmoid lines are not layers, so they are not counted.
blocks.end: So the four Linear lines are the three hidden layers and the output layer.

blocks.main: **The training lines make a guess, measure how wrong it is and change the weights.** **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, which updates each weight by a small step in the direction that reduces the error. **lr** is the learning rate, which determines how big each step is. The **loss** is the mistake, a number for how wrong the guess was.
sub: **backward** runs backpropagation, and **step** updates the weights.
**A higher learning rate learns faster but less accurately. A lower learning rate learns more accurately but more slowly.**

questions.q: How many hidden layers does this network have: Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 5)?
questions.a: This network has three hidden layers, with 3, 2 and 4 neurons. This is because it has five layers in all, the input layer, three hidden layers and the output layer, but only four Linear lines. The input layer does no processing, so it gets no line. The last line, Linear(4, 5), is the output layer. That leaves the first three lines as the three hidden layers.

questions.q: Write the code for the network with an additional hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output layer, and adjust the other layers.
questions.a: The code for the network with an extra hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output layer is Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 3), Linear(3, 5). To get it, keep the first three lines the same. Change the old last line from Linear(4, 5) to Linear(4, 3), so it becomes the new hidden layer of 3 neurons. Then add a new last line, Linear(3, 5), as the output layer. This works because every layer still takes in exactly as many numbers as the layer before it produces.

questions.q: Add a hidden layer of 6 neurons right after the input instead. What changes?
questions.a: Adding a hidden layer of 6 neurons right after the input changes the first line to Linear(2, 6) and adds a new second line, Linear(6, 3). The new second line takes the 6 numbers from the new layer and feeds them into the old first hidden layer of 3 neurons. The rest stays the same. So the network is Linear(2, 6), Linear(6, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4), Linear(4, 5).

questions.q: A network is written Linear(4, 3), Linear(3, 5), Linear(5, 2), Linear(2, 4). How many hidden layers, inputs and outputs does it have?
questions.a:
This network has three hidden layers, with 3, 5 and 2 neurons. This is because the last line, Linear(2, 4), is the output layer, and the three lines before it are hidden layers.

It has 4 inputs. This is because the first number on the first line, Linear(4, 3), is 4, so the network takes in 4 numbers.

It has 4 outputs. This is because the second number on the last line, Linear(2, 4), is 4. So it has 4 output neurons, and it decides among 4 categories.

questions.q: How many hidden layers does a network have if its code is Linear(2, 3), Sigmoid, Linear(3, 2), Sigmoid, Linear(2, 4), Sigmoid, Linear(4, 5)?
questions.a: A network with that code still has three hidden layers. This is because Sigmoid lines are not layers. They only apply the sigmoid to the numbers coming out of the layer before them. The sigmoid is a function that turns each number into a number between 0 and 1. So only the four Linear lines count, and the last one is the output layer. That leaves three hidden layers.

questions.q: What do the import lines do, and what does Sequential mean?
questions.a:
The import lines bring the torch library into Python. This means the programs for inner products and backpropagation do not have to be written by hand.

Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another. Each layer takes its input from the layer before it.

questions.q: What happens if the learning rate is raised from 0.1 to 0.3?
questions.a: If the learning rate is raised from 0.1 to 0.3, the network learns faster, but its accuracy goes down. This is because the learning rate determines how big each step in the weights is. A larger learning rate takes bigger steps, so the network gets close to the answer quickly. But the steps are big enough that it keeps going past the answer. So learning is faster, but less accurate.

questions.q: Two learning curves differ only in learning rate. One rises fast and jumps around, and the other rises slowly and smoothly. Which used the larger learning rate?
questions.a: The curve that rises fast and jumps around used the larger learning rate. This is because a larger learning rate takes bigger steps. Bigger steps get near the answer quickly, but they keep going past it, so that curve jumps around. Smaller steps are slower, so the other curve rises slowly but smoothly.

topics.title: From the vowel network to an LLM: many vectors in, the next item out

blocks.main: **An LLM (large language model) is given a sequence of vectors (lists of numbers) and predicts the next one.** For example, it is given 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth. The sixteenth is a probability distribution (a list of how likely each option is) over what could come next, such as each of about 30,000 English words.
sub: The vectors can be words, frames of a spectrogram (short time slices of a display of a sound's frequencies), patches of an image or the amino acids of a protein.
The LLM only ever works with lists of numbers, so the same design works for all of them.

blocks.main: **Language depends on connections between words that are far apart.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, ...", the next word is **barks**. Barks goes with the singular word dog, no matter how many words come in between.
sub: An LLM learns this from data, not from a rule someone teaches it.

blocks.main: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word, such as mat after "the cat sat on the".** When the prediction is wrong, backpropagation adjusts the weights. This is repeated with a huge number of sentences.
sub: Underneath everything, **inference** (using the network to make a prediction) is done with inner products. Learning is done with stochastic gradient descent plus **dynamic programming** (reusing calculations already done, which is how backpropagation works backward through the layers).
An LLM predicts from past data. So when something is not covered by its data, it can make things up, which is called **hallucination**.

questions.q: What is the difference between the input and output of the vowel network and those of an LLM?
questions.a:
The difference is that the vowel network takes in one vector and decides among five categories, while an LLM takes in many vectors and decides among a whole vocabulary.

The vowel network's input is one vector, F1 and F2. Its output decides among five categories.

An LLM's input is many vectors in sequence, such as the words so far. Its output decides among a whole vocabulary for the next item.

questions.q: An LLM is given 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth. Name three things the vectors can stand for.
questions.a: Three things the vectors can stand for are the words of a sentence, the frames of a spectrogram and the patches of an image. They can also stand for the amino acids of a protein. The same kind of prediction works for all of them. This is because the LLM only works with lists of numbers, whatever those numbers stand for.

questions.q: What does the sixteenth vector look like, and does it add up to anything?
questions.a:
The sixteenth vector is a probability distribution over what could come next, and its numbers add up to one.

The sixteenth vector has one number for each possible next item, such as each English word. Each number is how likely that item is to come next.

It adds up to one because it is a probability distribution. The probabilities of all the possible next items always add up to one.

questions.q: Why is the next word barks and not bark in "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, ... "?
questions.a: The next word is barks and not bark because barks goes with the singular word dog. This is true no matter how many words come in between. It holds even when the plural word parents comes in between. To predict barks, an LLM has to use a word far back in the sequence. It learns to do this from data, by computing inner products layer after layer.

questions.q: Why can an LLM hallucinate?
questions.a: An LLM can hallucinate because it predicts from past data. When it meets something its data does not cover, its prediction can turn into a guess. So it can make things up, and this is called hallucination.

topics.title: Phonotactics and guessing the next letter

blocks.main: **Phonotactics are the rules for which sounds can follow which in a language.** Every speaker knows them without being taught. A simple English syllable is a consonant, a vowel and a consonant, as in **Don** or **cup**.
sub: Mat, sit, dog, fish and shave are also consonant, vowel, consonant.
The pattern is about sounds, not letters. So the silent e at the end of shave does not count, because it makes no sound.
Ship, chin and bath also count. This is because sh, ch and th are each one sound, even though each is spelled with two letters.

blocks.main: **Consonants can also form clusters (groups of consonants in a row) before or after the vowel.** A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat, black and glad. A cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help, milk and lamp.
sub: The order of the consonants is a mirror image around the vowel. For example, l sits right next to the vowel in both flat and help. So flat is a word, and lfat is impossible.
Each real word has an impossible version that puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel, such as help and hepl, or lamp and lapm.
Sblit and desb are impossible too. That is why a product called desb would sound un-English.

blocks.main: **A pair of consonants can be fine across a syllable break but impossible at the start of a syllable.** Atlantic is a word because t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break (At-lan-tic). Tlantic is impossible because tl cannot start an English syllable.
sub: The sound ng can end a syllable, but it can never start one.

blocks.main: **Each language has its own phonotactics.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds (sounds made with air going out through the nose, like n and ng) at the end of a syllable. Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word.
sub: Spanish speakers add an e before st at the start of a word, as in estadio.

blocks.main: **Guessing the next letter of a word depends on phonotactics, and each guess is a probability distribution.** After a vowel, almost any letter can come next, so the distribution is **flat** (the probability is spread out over many letters). At the start of a word, the choices narrow down to what an English onset allows.
sub: After ra, almost any letter can come next, such as t, n, r or l, so the distribution is flat.
After skr, the distribution is **sharply peaked** (most of the probability goes to a few vowels).
blocks.end: So a GPT trained only on this guessing game learns English syllable structure. This is because guessing the next letter is the same task as an LLM predicting the sixteenth item from the first fifteen.

blocks.main: **At the start of a word, each first letter or cluster allows only a few next letters.** After sp, only l, r or a vowel can come next, never n. After k, a vowel or n can come next, as in knee, but never t.
sub: After b or f, only r, l or a vowel can come next, never n.
After sh, only a vowel or r can come next, as in shrimp.
After skr, or after m at the start of a word, only a vowel can come next.

blocks.main: **Inside a word, the letters so far can make one next letter almost certain.** After bram, the next letter is almost certainly b, as in bramble.
sub: A new syllable could also start there, so b is not the only possible next letter.

blocks.main: **After pl, st and th at the start of a word, the next letter is limited too.** After pl, only a vowel can come next, as in play. After st, a vowel or r can come next, as in star and street, but not l or k.
sub: After th, r, w or a vowel can come next, as in three, thwart and thin, but not l or n.

questions.q: Which could be English words: blick, bnick, sblat, splat, dlag, lisk, lisb, lapm, lamp? For each one that could not, name the problem.
questions.a:
Blick, splat, lisk and lamp could be English words.

Bnick, sblat and dlag could not be English words. This is because bn, sb and dl cannot start a syllable in English.

Lisb and lapm could not be English words. This is because sb and pm cannot end a syllable in English.

questions.q: Each of these starts an English word: pl_, st_ and th_. What could come next, and what could not?
questions.a:
After pl, only a vowel can come next, as in play. So a consonant such as n cannot come next.

After st, a vowel or r can come next, as in star and street. But l and k cannot come next.

After th, r, w or a vowel can come next, as in three, thwart and thin. But l and n cannot come next.

questions.q: After which start is the next-letter distribution flatter, ra_ or skr_? Why?
questions.a: The next-letter distribution is flatter after ra than after skr. This is because ra ends in a vowel, and after a vowel almost any letter can come next. So the probability is spread out over many letters. After skr, only a vowel can come next. So most of the probability goes to a few vowels, and the distribution is sharply peaked.

questions.q: Why is Atlantic an English word but tlantic impossible?
questions.a: Atlantic is an English word, but tlantic is impossible. This is because in Atlantic, the t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break (At-lan-tic), so each syllable follows the rules. In tlantic, tl would have to start a syllable. English does not allow tl at the start of a syllable, so tlantic is impossible.

questions.q: Could ngop be an English word? Could flim?
questions.a:
Ngop could not be an English word. This is because the sound ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.

Flim could be an English word. This is because fl is an allowed onset (the consonants before the vowel), as in flat, and im is an allowed ending.

questions.q: Why does a GPT trained only to guess the next letter end up knowing English syllable structure?
questions.a: A GPT trained only to guess the next letter ends up knowing English syllable structure because the patterns of English syllables determine which letters can come next. This is because its guesses can only get better by matching those patterns. So as it learns, its probability distributions take on the shape of those patterns. They are flat after a vowel and sharply peaked after a start such as skr.

questions.q: Which letter cannot come next after sp_ at the start of a word: l, r, n or a?
questions.a: N cannot come next after sp at the start of a word. This is because spn is not an allowed English onset (the consonants before the vowel). After sp, only l, r or a vowel can come next, as in split, spring and spa.

questions.q: Which letter cannot come next after k_ at the start of a word: a, n or t?
questions.a: T cannot come next after k at the start of a word. This is because kt cannot start an English syllable. After k, a vowel or n can come next, as in knee.

questions.q: What can come next after b_ or f_ at the start of a word, and what cannot?
questions.a: After b or f at the start of a word, only r, l or a vowel can come next, as in bring, black, frog and flat. N cannot come next. This is because bn and fn cannot start an English syllable.

questions.q: What can come next after sh_ at the start of a word?
questions.a: After sh at the start of a word, only a vowel or r can come next, as in ship and shrimp. This is because shr is the only consonant cluster that English allows starting with sh.

questions.q: What can come next after skr_?
questions.a: After skr, only a vowel can come next, as in scream and scrap (where the skr sound is spelled scr). This is because skr already fills the whole onset (the consonants before the vowel). So no other consonant can be added before the vowel.

questions.q: Why are lfat, hepl and lapm impossible when flat, help and lamp are words?
questions.a: Lfat, hepl and lapm are impossible because the order of a cluster is a mirror image around the vowel. In flat and help, the l sits right next to the vowel. In lamp, the m sits right next to the vowel. Each impossible version puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel. So it breaks the mirror order, and it cannot be an English word.

questions.q: Is ship a consonant, vowel, consonant word even though it has four letters?
questions.a: Yes, ship is a consonant, vowel, consonant word even though it has four letters. This is because the pattern is about sounds, not letters, and sh is one sound. So ship is the consonant sh, the vowel i and the consonant p.

topics.title: Harmonics and formants: fixed-fixed and fixed-free systems

blocks.ref: Lecture 11 · p8 · Lecture 12 · p8, 10 · Lecture 13 · p4, 5
blocks.main: **In a system fixed at both ends, such as a string or the vocal folds, neither end can move.** Its first mode (the simplest way the system can vibrate) is **half a wave** stretched between the two fixed ends. Each higher mode has to fit a whole number of these half-waves between the ends.
sub: Mode N contains N copies of Mode 1, so its frequency (how many times per second it vibrates) is N times the first frequency.
These modes at **1, 2, 3, 4 times** the first frequency are called **harmonics**.
For example, if Mode 1 is 200 Hz, then Mode 5 is five times 200 Hz, which is 1,000 Hz.
blocks.end: So in a fixed-fixed system, the modes are spaced apart by the first frequency.

blocks.ref: Lecture 11 · p9 · Lecture 12 · p12 · Lecture 13 · p6 · Lecture 14 · p2
blocks.main: **A membrane such as the vocal folds vibrates across a surface, and it can vibrate in several modes at the same time.** A single point on the membrane moves in every mode that has motion at that point. A **spectrum** separates this combined vibration back into its separate modes.
sub: A spectrum shows frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude (strength) on the vertical axis.
It has one spike for each mode that is present. For example, if Mode 1 is 200 Hz, Modes 1 to 6 give spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 Hz.
blocks.end: So a spectrum shows which modes are present and how strong each one is.

blocks.main: **A scientific theory is tested by checking whether its prediction comes true.** The theory says the vocal folds are a membrane. This theory predicts **equidistant harmonics** (harmonics that are evenly spaced in frequency).
sub: To test it, a vowel is recorded, and its spectrum is checked in **Praat** (a program for analyzing speech sounds) to see whether the peaks are evenly spaced.
The recordings showed evenly spaced harmonics, so the prediction was confirmed.
blocks.end: So the theory that the vocal folds are a membrane passed its test.

blocks.ref: Lecture 11 · p11 · Lecture 12 · p14 · Lecture 13 · p7, 8, 9 · Lecture 14 · p3, 4
blocks.main: **A fixed-free system is held still at one end and free to move at the other end.** A **building** is fixed to the ground and free at the top. The **air in the vocal tract** works the same way. It is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips.
sub: The first mode is a **quarter-wave packet** (one quarter of a wave). It goes from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end.
The free end must always be moving. Because of this, packets have to be added two at a time, which gives one, three, five and seven packets.
So the modes come at **1, 3, 5, 7 times** the first frequency, and these modes are called **formants**.
blocks.end: So fixed-free modes are spaced apart by **twice** the first frequency, while fixed-fixed modes are spaced apart by the first frequency.

questions.q: A string is fixed on both sides. If Mode 1 has frequency 200 Hz, what frequency does Mode 5 have?
questions.a: Mode 5 has a frequency of 1000 Hz. This is because in a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a whole-number multiple of the first mode. Mode 5 contains five copies of Mode 1. So the frequency of Mode 5 is five times 200 Hz, which is 1000 Hz.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends has Mode 1 at 150 Hz. What are Modes 2 and 3? If one end is freed and Mode 1 stays at 150 Hz, what are Modes 2 and 3 now?
questions.a:
When the string is fixed at both ends, Mode 2 is 300 Hz and Mode 3 is 450 Hz. This is because a system fixed at both ends has modes at every whole-number multiple of the first. Mode 2 is two times 150 Hz, and Mode 3 is three times 150 Hz. So these modes are 150 Hz apart.

When one end is freed, Mode 2 is 450 Hz and Mode 3 is 750 Hz. This is because a system fixed at one end and free at the other has only the odd multiples of the first frequency. Mode 2 is three times 150 Hz, and Mode 3 is five times 150 Hz. So these modes are 300 Hz apart.

questions.q: Why are the frequencies of fixed-fixed vibratory systems spaced the way they are?
questions.a: The frequencies of fixed-fixed vibratory systems are spaced evenly, as whole-number multiples of the first frequency. This is because every mode has to fit a whole number of half-waves between the two ends that cannot move. The first mode is half a wave. It goes from no motion at one end, to the most motion in the middle, and back to no motion at the other end. Mode 2 fits two half-waves into the same length, so it vibrates twice as fast. Mode 3 fits three half-waves, so it vibrates three times as fast. Since each mode adds one more half-wave, the spacing between the frequencies stays even.

questions.q: Why are the formants of a fixed-free system 1, 3, 5, etc. multiples of the base frequency?
questions.a: The formants of a fixed-free system are 1, 3, 5, etc. multiples of the base frequency because every mode must start with no motion at the fixed end and end with the most motion at the free end. The basic piece is a quarter-wave packet (one quarter of a wave). It goes from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end. Adding just one more packet would leave a point with no motion at the free end, and that cannot happen. So packets are added two at a time, which gives one, three, five and seven packets. That is why the formant frequencies are odd multiples of the base frequency.

questions.q: If F1 is 500 Hz, what are F2 and F3?
questions.a: If F1 (the first formant) is 500 Hz, then F2 is 1500 Hz and F3 is 2500 Hz. This is because the air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system. In a fixed-free system, the formants are odd multiples of the first formant. So F2 is three times 500 Hz, and F3 is five times 500 Hz. They are not two times and three times 500 Hz.

questions.q: What aspect of speech has the properties in the fixed-free question?
questions.a: The formants of the air in the vocal tract have the properties in the fixed-free question. This is because the air in the vocal tract is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips. A system like this vibrates only at odd multiples of its first frequency. So the formants (the frequencies at which the air in the vocal tract vibrates) are odd multiples of the first formant.

questions.q: What aspect of speech has frequencies at whole-number multiples, and why?
questions.a: The harmonics of the vocal folds are at whole-number multiples of the first frequency. This is because the vocal folds are a membrane held in place along their edges. So they behave like a system fixed at both ends. In a system fixed at both ends, each mode is a whole number of copies of the first mode. That is why the harmonics are at whole-number multiples.

questions.q: What in speech is a building analogous to, and why does the analogy hold?
questions.a: A building is analogous to the air in the vocal tract. This is because both are fixed at one end and free at the other end. The building is fixed to the ground and free at the top. The air in the vocal tract is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips. Since the ends match, both are most springy at the fixed end, where they are stretched or compressed the most. Both also move the most at the free end, and both have frequencies at odd multiples of the first frequency. That is why the analogy holds.

questions.q: How is a building different from the air in the vocal tract?
questions.a: A building is different from the air in the vocal tract because a building is designed to sway only in Mode 1. The air in the vocal tract vibrates in all of its modes at the same time. Engineers avoid the higher modes in a building. This is because higher modes would move floors in opposite directions, and that could break the structure. In speech, all the modes are used. Speaking changes the mass and stiffness of the air at different locations in the vocal tract, so the formants move.

questions.q: Draw the spectrum for a string fixed at both ends with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 6.
questions.a: The spectrum for a string fixed at both ends with Mode 1 at 200 Hz has six evenly spaced spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 and 1200 Hz. There is one spike for each mode. Frequency goes along the horizontal axis, and amplitude (strength) goes up the vertical axis. The spikes are evenly spaced because a string fixed at both ends has its modes at whole-number multiples of Mode 1. If the modes are equally strong, the spikes can be drawn at the same height.

questions.q: Draw the spectrum for a fixed-free system with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 4.
questions.a: The spectrum for a fixed-free system with Mode 1 at 200 Hz has spikes only at the odd multiples, which are 200, 600, 1000 and 1400 Hz. This is because a fixed-free system has no even multiples. An even number of quarter-wave packets would leave a point with no motion at the free end. The free end must always be moving, so only odd numbers of packets are possible. That is why the four spikes are at 1, 3, 5 and 7 times 200 Hz.

questions.q: If the vocal folds have their base frequency, F0, at 150 Hz, draw the spectrum for the first 5 harmonics.
questions.a: The spectrum for the first 5 harmonics has spikes at 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz. This is because the vocal folds are a membrane fixed along its edges. So their harmonics are whole-number multiples of F0 (the base frequency), and the spikes are evenly spaced, 150 Hz apart. Frequency goes along the horizontal axis, and amplitude (strength) goes up the vertical axis.

topics.title: Backpropagation: why learning starts at the end

blocks.main: **Every neural network starts with random weights and learns by correcting its mistakes, one small step at a time.** **Backpropagation** is the method that figures out how each weight should change. **The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last.**
sub: The last weights affect the output probabilities **directly**. So one inner product (multiplying each input by its weight and adding the results) shows whether each last weight should go up or down.
A first-layer weight affects the first hidden layer. That layer affects the next layer, and that layer affects the one after it.
So the effect of a first-layer weight passes through every layer, and it depends on all the later weights.
blocks.end: So learning starts at the end and works backward toward the input.

blocks.main: **Dynamic programming solves the easy problem first and then reuses its answer to solve the bigger problem that contains it.** This idea comes from **Bellman** and **Viterbi**. In backpropagation, the easy problem is the last layer. The bigger problem includes every earlier layer.
sub: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.**
Stochastic gradient descent (**SGD**) changes each weight by a small amount. Dynamic programming determines the order in which the weights are changed.

blocks.main: **Backpropagation was worked out in the mid-1980s.** Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.
sub: The idea of backpropagation is at the center of much of today's economy.

questions.q: In what order are the weights updated?
questions.a: The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last. This is because the update for each layer reuses the calculations already made for the layers after it. The last layer has no layers after it, so it can be worked out first. Each earlier layer then uses those calculations. So the updates go in order from the last weights back to the first.

questions.q: Why does backpropagation start at the end?
questions.a:
Backpropagation starts at the end because the last weights are the simplest problem. This is because the last weights affect the output probabilities (the network's decision) directly. So it is easy to tell whether raising or lowering each last weight makes the loss (the error) go up or down.

A weight from the input to the first hidden layer is harder. It affects the first, second and third hidden layers before it reaches the output. So changing it is a very complex problem, and that problem contains the problem of changing the last weights.

Backpropagation follows dynamic programming, so it solves the simplest problem first. That answer then makes each harder problem easier, until the most complex problem is solved. That is why backpropagation starts with the last weights.

questions.q: What two methods together train the network's weights?
questions.a: The two methods that together train the network's weights are stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation. This is because each method does a different job. Backpropagation works backward from the error to figure out which direction each weight should change. Stochastic gradient descent then changes each weight by a small step in that direction. Together, these two steps update the weights.

questions.q: Backpropagation is made of what two parts?
questions.a: Backpropagation is made of two parts, stochastic gradient descent and dynamic programming. Stochastic gradient descent changes each weight by a small step in the direction that reduces the error. Dynamic programming determines the order of the changes. The order goes from the last weights back to the first weights.

questions.q: Which part of training is the SGD part, and which is the dynamic programming part? What are the small problem and the big problem?
questions.a:
The SGD part is updating the weights. Each weight takes a small step in the direction that reduces the error, and the learning rate determines how big that step is.

The dynamic programming part is calculating how much each weight contributed to the error. It starts with the last layer and uses those calculations to work backward through the earlier layers.

The small problem is figuring out how the weights in the last layer contributed to the error. The big problem is figuring out how the weights in the earlier layers contributed to the error.

questions.q: The network said done but the answer was dean. Should a last weight that pushes done up go up or down? Why?
questions.a: A last weight that makes the probability of done go up should go down. This is because the correct answer was dean, so the desired output for done is zero. The network gave done a probability that is too high. Lowering this weight makes the amount it adds to done smaller. So the probability of done goes down toward zero.

questions.q: If the network already makes the right decision on a recording, what does it learn from it?
questions.a: If the network already makes the right decision on a recording, it learns nothing from that recording. This is because there is no error to correct, so the weights do not change. This can be a problem, because a network can keep getting the right answers by memorizing its data, without learning the pattern underneath. Once it gets everything right, it has no errors left to learn from.

topics.title: Leading up to LLMs: from one neuron to networks that unfold over time

blocks.main: **A neuron in an artificial neural network takes in a vector (a list of numbers) and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results. This is called the **inner product**. A **neural network** repeats the inner product layer after layer.
sub: A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions.

blocks.main: **Artificial neural networks began in biology, not in technology.** The first paper on artificial neural networks was by **McCulloch and Pitts**. It started from the all-or-none behavior of real neurons. A real neuron is either firing or not firing. This is the same idea as the **sigmoid** (a function that turns a number into a value between 0 and 1).
sub: The earliest neural network work tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness.
In the **Parallel Distributed Processing** books, **parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.
**Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. By the time these books were written, forward propagation and backpropagation were well worked out.

blocks.main: **The vowel network takes one static vector and makes one decision.** A **static** vector is a fixed list of numbers from one moment in time. But speech changes all the time, and a sentence is many words, one after another.
sub: So one fixed list of numbers cannot model thinking that unfolds over time.

blocks.main: **A recurrent network sends its own output back into part of its input, so what it produces at one moment helps predict the next moment.** **Michael Jordan** built the **recurrent** network to model speech production. He built it because features such as nasality and lip rounding switch on and off at different moments.
sub: **Plan units** hold what the network is supposed to say, and **state units** hold a copy of the last output. Both send their values to the hidden layer, and the hidden layer sends its values to the output.
The output is copied back into the state units. The same weights are used at every step.
blocks.end: So a recurrent network can work through a sequence, instead of handling only one static vector.

blocks.main: **GPT works the same way as the recurrent network, one word at a time.** It predicts the next word and adds that word to the prompt. Then it uses the whole prompt, including the new word, as input to predict the word after that.
sub: The main steps in this history are 1943 (the McCulloch and Pitts paper), 1985 (backpropagation) and 2017 (the design behind GPT).

questions.q: How does the all-or-none behavior of neurons connect to the sigmoid?
questions.a: The all-or-none behavior of neurons is the same idea as the sigmoid. This is because a real neuron is either firing or not firing. The sigmoid turns an inner product into a number near 0 (off) or near 1 (on), with a steep change in between. So an artificial neuron that uses the sigmoid behaves the same way as a real neuron.

questions.q: What do parallel and distributed mean in Parallel Distributed Processing?
questions.a:
Parallel means that many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.

Distributed means that the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. So the information is not stored in one place.

questions.q: What does a single neuron take in and give back? What about a neural network?
questions.a:
A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number. That number is the inner product, which is each input multiplied by its weight, with the results added together.

A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions. This is because a neural network repeats the inner product layer after layer. So the network ends with several outputs instead of just one number.

questions.q: Why can't the vowel network model a sentence or speech over time?
questions.a: The vowel network cannot model a sentence or speech over time because it takes one static vector and makes one decision. That vector is F1 and F2 (the first two formants) from one moment. But speech changes all the time, and a sentence is many words, one after another. So modeling speech needs a network that works through a sequence.

questions.q: What makes Jordan's network recurrent, and why did he build it?
questions.a:
Jordan's network is recurrent because it sends its own output back into part of its input. It copies the output into the state units. So what it produced at one moment helps predict the next moment.

Jordan built it because speech production changes over time. Features such as nasality and lip rounding switch on and off at different moments. So he needed a network that could follow these changes step by step.

questions.q: How is a recurrent network different from an nn.Sequential network?
questions.a: A recurrent network is different from an nn.Sequential network because it loops its output back into its input. A Sequential network passes the input through the layers once, from the input to the output, and makes one decision. A recurrent network sends its output back in as part of its next input. So a recurrent network works through a sequence step by step.

questions.q: How does GPT use the same idea as Jordan's network?
questions.a: GPT uses the same idea as Jordan's network because it also feeds its own output back into its input. It predicts the next word and adds that word to the prompt. Then it predicts again, using the longer prompt. So GPT produces text one word at a time.

topics.title: The LLM as a dynamical system

blocks.main: **A dynamical system is a rule that is given its own output as input again and again.** Numbers go in, the rule changes them, and new numbers come out. The output then becomes the next input.
sub: In the **harmonic oscillator** (a mass on a spring moving back and forth), the two numbers are position and velocity (speed and direction). They take turns updating.
When the rule is repeated step by step, the position traces out a **cosine** shape.

blocks.main: **An LLM (large language model) can be treated as a dynamical system.** Each layer is the rule, and the depth of the layers plays the role of time. The input vectors are the **initial conditions** (the starting numbers).
sub: Each layer turns the vectors into better vectors, until the last layer can predict the next word.
Each layer has its own learned weights. So each step passes its output to the next step, but each step uses different weights.
blocks.end: So in both systems, the output of one step is the input to the next step.

questions.q: Why is an LLM called a dynamical system?
questions.a: An LLM is called a dynamical system because it works by giving a rule its own output again and again. A dynamical system is a rule that is repeatedly given its own output as input, starting from initial conditions (the starting numbers). In an LLM, the input vectors are the initial conditions. Each layer applies its weights to turn those vectors into better vectors, and the next layer takes those as its input. So the depth of the layers plays the role of time.

questions.q: In the harmonic oscillator, which two numbers update, and in what order?
questions.a: In the harmonic oscillator, position x and velocity v update, and they take turns. First, the new x is calculated from the old v. Then, the new v is calculated from the new x. When these two steps are repeated over and over, x traces out a cosine shape.

topics.title: The vocal tract, constrictions and the vowels /i/, /a/ and /u/

blocks.main: **The air in the vocal tract vibrates back and forth along the tube, and it is a fixed-free system.** This means it has one end where the air cannot move and one end where it can. The air is **fixed at the glottis** (the opening between the vocal folds). The closed vocal folds stop the air there from moving, so the air there can only be compressed. The air is **free at the lips**, where it moves in and out.
sub: When the air on both sides of a spot moves toward that spot, the air at that spot gets compressed (packed together). When the air on both sides moves away from the spot, the air there spreads out.
This means the spot where the air moves the least is the spot where it gets compressed the most. The spot where the air moves the most is the spot where it gets compressed the least.
When there is no constriction, as in **done**, the vowel is **schwa** (the neutral vowel sound). Its formants (frequency regions with strong acoustic energy) are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**.
blocks.end: So a constriction does different things depending on where it is placed, because the air moves differently at different places in the tube.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p16 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8
blocks.main: **In the vocal tract, vowels differ in the shape of the tube.** The shape depends on where the tongue makes a constriction and whether the lips are rounded.
